newsitem.title: GUATEMALA: Guatemala truth commission seeks funds.
newsitem.headline: Guatemala truth commission seeks funds.

text.p: Guatemala's truth commission has been entrusted with investigating 36 years of dirty war massacres and assassinations but given too little money to do its work, its director said.

German law professor Christian Tomuschat, head of the commission, told Reuters the panel will not be able to start work as scheduled in June unless it gets more funding. "We can start if we get just a part of the money we need," he said.

Leftist Guatemalan National Revolutionary Unit (URNG) rebels and the government signed an agreement in December that ended 36 years of civil war. International donors have promised more than $1 billion to fulfil the accords but the government has earmarked only $50,000 for the commission.

"$50,000 is, of course, very little. It was clear the commission would entail a much bigger cost," said Tomuschat, who has met ambassadors from Europe and the United States to ask for $8 million in donations.

He said the government has talked about giving the peace commission more money but has done nothing. Members of the government's presidential peace secretariat, which oversees the peace budget, were not available for comment.

Under terms of the accords signed on Dec. 29 the three-member commission -- the other two members are Guatemalan -- will spend between six and 12 months documenting human rights violations. Even though it has not yet started its work, the commission is already a source of controversy in the country, where an estimated 100,000 people died and another 40,000 disappeared during the fighting.

Human rights leaders and relatives of the victims have criticised the commission because of its mandate says it should not "individualize responsibility" -- a euphemism for naming those responsible for abuse.

Many victims blame high-ranking members of the military and want the commission to name names. But army leaders have made it clear that to them the spirit of the accords meant "you should not put names in the report," Tomuschat said.
"Institutional responsibility must be clearly indicated ... but if we only said it was the army, or the URNG, probably that would be too little," he said.
The commission also will try to determine the real number of victims. "We should at least make an attempt at verifying those numbers. I don't know whether that will be possible."

Tomuschat called the investigation of 36 years of war in less than a year an "almost impossible" task for the small commission. But he said it will use testimony gathered previously by the Catholic church and other groups.
